summary: Dana Point sits on one of the few stretches of Southern California coastline where the bluffs actually rise high enough to let you look *down* onto migrating gray whales from dry land — the headlands here drop roughly 100 feet to the Pacific, and the harbor below is one of only a handful of whale-watching ports between Santa Barbara and San Diego. That setting is genuinely dramatic, but the price tag matches: a median home value near $1.2 million against a median household income of about $127,000 yields a price-to-income ratio above 9, meaning even well-compensated households face a steep buy-in, and the $2,883 median rent claims over a quarter of that median income before taxes. The town is compact — barely seven square miles — and functions largely as a bedroom community; most employment draws from the broader south Orange County corridor in healthcare, hospitality, and professional services, so commuting north on I-5 or the Pacific Coast Highway is the norm. Daily weather barely fluctuates, averaging a 70°F high with nine hours of sunshine year-round, which makes the excellent coastal trail network from the harbor up through the blufftop paths genuinely usable every day. The food and retail scene clusters along a small commercial stretch near the harbor and along Del Prado Avenue — more independent sit-down restaurants and coffee spots than chain-heavy sprawl, giving the town a distinct identity within Orange County's long suburban coastline. Dana Point is essentially a place where the geography is extraordinary and the economics are relentless, and deciding between those two facts is the entire conversation.
